content: The analysis conducted in 2018 focused on determining whether monthly culture testing, monthly smear microscopy, or culture testing every two months was necessary to avoid missing treatment failure in patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) undergoing treatment. Approximately 60% of the patients included in the study were people living with HIV (PLHIV). However, the data did not address the impact of these testing frequencies on the acquisition or amplification of additional drug resistance. Furthermore, it could not directly assess whether the frequency of culture or smear microscopy testing had an equivalent effect on treatment failure in patients receiving the 9–12-month shorter MDR-TB regimen, as outlined in the original PICO question. The certainty of the evidence regarding test accuracy was rated as moderate, based on predefined criteria documented in GRADEpro. An individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis compared the sensitivity and specificity of the two testing methods, as well as the performance of monthly culture testing versus culture testing every two months. The goal was to determine the minimum testing frequency required to avoid unnecessary delays in revising treatment regimens. Monthly culture testing was found to increase the detection of true positive bacteriological results by 13 per 1,000 patients and reduce false negative results by the same margin when compared to sputum smear microscopy alone. However, monthly culture testing also resulted in 17 fewer true negative results and 17 more false positive results per 1,000 patients, potentially leading to prolonged treatment in cases of false positivity or missed true negativity. The inconvenience to patients and healthcare programs associated with monthly culture testing was considered relatively minor, as sputum collection and other biological specimen collection are typically non-invasive and routine in many programs. In settings where monthly testing is implemented, a single false positive result is unlikely to harm the patient significantly, as WHO guidelines recommend basing treatment decisions on at least two consecutive positive results to confirm prolonged positivity or reversion. The impact of a single spurious result would be limited to the time until the next test, typically one month later. No clear threshold was identified at which the odds of treatment failure increased sharply when monitoring with either sputum smear microscopy or culture testing. The decision to change treatment regimens depends on the clinician’s preference to minimize the risk of failure and avoid prolonging a failing regimen. The IPD meta-analysis included 3,762 patients with clinical characteristics similar to the 22,760 individuals excluded from the analysis, although the included patients were slightly less likely to be HIV co-infected, have a history of previous treatment, or exhibit second-line drug resistance. Subgroup considerations suggested that the findings could apply to other key patient groups, including those on longer MDR-TB regimens, regardless of the number of Group A, B, or C agents used or the inclusion of an injectable intensive phase. For patients under 15 years of age with MDR/RR-TB, who comprised less than 2% of the IPD meta-analysis, culture testing may be more sensitive than smear microscopy due to the typically low bacterial load in their specimens. However, monthly testing may not be feasible in children unable to produce sputum spontaneously, as it would require invasive procedures like gastric aspirates or induced sputum collection. Similarly, for patients with extrapulmonary TB, culture testing is more likely to detect persistent disease due to the paucibacillary nature of the condition, although sample collection can be challenging. Direct microscopy should still be attempted, as it can provide faster results than culture. HIV-negative individuals with TB generally have higher bacterial counts in their sputum, making smear microscopy more effective in this population. However, past studies have supported the joint use of both microscopy and culture, preferably monthly, even in low HIV-prevalence settings. Patients on shorter MDR-TB regimens, which involve a shorter intensive phase and total treatment duration, may require less frequent culture testing. However, programs implementing shorter regimens should aim for more frequent culture testing, especially after the intensive phase, to confirm bacteriological cure and investigate any signs of recurrence after treatment completion. Good-quality sputum specimens are essential for accurate TB diagnosis, and laboratories must have adequate space and resources to ensure quality, safety, and efficiency. Some countries face challenges in implementing and maintaining quality assurance for sputum culture, which affects the feasibility of this recommendation. The quality of sputum specimens and their proper transport to laboratories are critical to maintaining the viability of the bacilli and obtaining valid culture results. The use of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay for monitoring treatment response has not yet been determined. Implementing more frequent microbiological testing would require additional resources for both laboratories and patients, who may face increased time and financial burdens. Patient values and preferences should be considered to ensure acceptable and patient-centered care delivery. Increased monitoring should not overburden laboratory services or compromise health equity by diverting resources from other essential program components. Culture and microscopy results for MDR-TB patients should be recorded in second-line TB treatment registers and laboratory registers, which may be part of electronic systems to facilitate real-time data access and reduce errors. Performance indicators, such as contamination rates and turnaround times, can help improve the quality of care. In cases of repeated positive cultures, repeat drug susceptibility testing is important. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is recommended for all HIV-positive patients with drug-resistant TB requiring second-line antituberculosis drugs, regardless of CD4 cell count, and should be initiated within the first eight weeks of starting TB treatment. Evidence from observational studies suggests that ART reduces the risk of death and increases the likelihood of cure in these patients. However, the quality of evidence is low to very low, and no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were available. The use of ART in patients with drug-resistant TB is supported by indirect evidence from its use in patients with drug-susceptible TB, which shows significant benefits, particularly in highly immunocompromised individuals. The timing of ART initiation in drug-resistant TB patients should follow the same approach as in drug-susceptible TB patients. Successful implementation of this recommendation will require more trained providers, increased access to treatment, and additional support for adherence. Updated information on drug-drug interactions between antiretroviral and antituberculosis medications is now available online. Elective partial lung resection, such as lobectomy or wedge resection, may be considered as an adjunct to recommended MDR-TB regimens in patients with rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB. Surgery has historically been used in TB treatment and remains an option in some settings. It may help reduce bacterial load and improve prognosis in cases of intractable pathology. The effectiveness of surgery as an adjunct to medical therapy was evaluated through an IPD meta-analysis and a systematic review.
